findings: 63 splits are GPT rejection / Decision-1 acceptance; 27 run in the opposite direction. The direction does not identify which evaluator is right.
38 examinations find no persuasive visible defect that explains the split. These remain unexplained, not proven-correct answers.
Analysts describe 21 apparent defects, 29 ambiguous cases and 40 defensible answers. These are qualitative post-hoc assessments, not independently labelled correctness results.

Recurring visible tensions concern whether conditional requirements apply, whether claimed source/workflow provenance is actually supplied, and whether cautious language or terse deliverables satisfy the exact scenario. Some tensions concern supporting provenance rather than the core business conclusion.
2 disagreements contain native Decision-1 exact ties. The rest cannot be reduced to that recorded tie mechanism. No new confidence cutoff or vote change follows from this observation.
limitations: Post-hoc AI analyst interpretations of saved evidence, not new independent evaluator votes.
Neither evaluator returned a rationale for these disagreements; their internal reasons are unknown.
Categories identify observable tensions or plausible interpretations, not established causes of a vote.
Analyst confidence is qualitative and uncalibrated; native Decision-1 confidence is a separate diagnostic.
No human reference labels establish which evaluator is correct. GPT is not ground truth.
Original answers, evaluator instructions, judgments, confidence policy and accounting are unchanged.
Analyst CLI work is not included in the original experiment's recorded model cost or timing.
